sections: How each Gospel opens, and the start of Jesus’ ministry.
The first calls, healings and conflicts in and around Capernaum.
The Sermon on the Mount and the Plain, and teaching that Matthew and Luke share.
Stories Jesus told about the kingdom.
Signs on the sea and on land, and the sending of the disciples.
From Peter’s confession to the road to Jerusalem.
The triumphal entry and the days of teaching in the temple.
The last discourse and the call to be ready.
From the plot to the burial.

m.s: Writes with a Jewish-Christian audience in view. Shows Jesus as the promised Son of David and a new Moses, quoting the prophets again and again ("this took place to fulfill"). Gathers Jesus’ teaching into five long discourses.

k.s: The shortest and quickest Gospel, full of vivid detail and action ("immediately"). Shows Jesus as the powerful Son of God who must suffer, and the disciples as slow to understand. Often explains Jewish customs for readers who did not know them.

l.s: Writes as a careful historian addressed to Theophilus. Emphasizes Jesus’ welcome of the poor, women, sinners and outsiders, and the work of the Holy Spirit and prayer. Often tells stories that only he preserves.

j.s: Selects a smaller number of "signs" and long conversations so that readers may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God (20:31). Rarely overlaps with the other three, and often fills in what they leave out.

groups.sh: Each Gospel opens by telling you who Jesus is, but they start in four different places.

m: Opens with a family record: "Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham."
k: One announcement, "the beginning of the gospel," then straight to John the Baptist. No birth story, no preface.
l: Opens with a careful preface to Theophilus: he investigated everything and wrote an orderly account.
j: Opens before creation: "In the beginning was the Word."

w.m: A Jewish-Christian reader needs to see first that Jesus is the promised Son of David and heir of Abraham.
w.k: Mark moves fast. There is no birth story and no preface; the good news begins with the action.
w.l: Luke writes like a historian, naming his method (investigation, careful order) so the reader can be certain.
w.j: John states at the start the claim the whole book sets out to prove (see John 20:31): Jesus is the eternal Word made flesh.

groups.sh: Both trace Jesus through the line of David, and both include Abraham.

m: Starts with Abraham and moves forward to Jesus, in three sets of fourteen.
Names four women (Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Uriah’s wife), and runs from David through Solomon.
l: Starts with Jesus and moves backward past Abraham to Adam, and then to God.

Names no women, and runs from David through Nathan. The two lists share only a few names after David. Interpreters suggest one follows Joseph’s legal line and the other Mary’s family, or that levirate marriage joins them; the Gospels do not say.

w.m: Placed first, to show a Jewish reader that Jesus fulfils the promises to Abraham and David. The women, several of them outsiders, quietly point toward grace reaching beyond Israel.
w.l: Placed after Jesus is called "my Son" at his baptism, and running back to Adam, it fits Luke’s theme that Jesus is Savior of the whole human family.

groups.sh: Jesus is born in Bethlehem to Mary, a virgin engaged to Joseph of David’s house, and is named Jesus at the angel’s word.

m: Told from Joseph’s side: dreams, the Magi, Herod’s rage, the escape to Egypt.
Family moves from Bethlehem to Egypt and then to Nazareth.
l: Told from Mary’s side: Gabriel, the census, shepherds, Simeon and Anna in the temple.
Family goes from Nazareth to Bethlehem for the census and back to Nazareth. Readers have long put the two accounts together as complementary.

w.m: Matthew shapes the story around Scripture ("this took place to fulfill") and echoes Moses: a threatened infant, a flight to Egypt, a return. Jesus is the new Moses and the true king.
w.l: Luke shows God lifting up the lowly: a young woman, shepherds, a manger, a widow and an old man. Joy, song and the Spirit fill the story.

groups.sh: John prepares the way in the wilderness, baptizes with water, and says someone stronger is coming.

m: Adds John’s sharp words to the Pharisees and Sadducees.
k: Shortest. Starts with a quotation from Isaiah (with a line from Malachi).
l: Dates the scene by emperors and governors, and adds practical advice to crowds, tax collectors and soldiers.
j: Skips the baptizing. Gives John’s answers to priests sent from Jerusalem: I am not the Christ, not Elijah, but a voice.

w.m: Matthew stresses repentance in view of the kingdom of heaven and warns religious leaders who rely on Abraham’s name.
w.k: Mark keeps it to the essentials: the forerunner and the stronger one who follows.
w.l: Luke places John in world history and shows what repentance looks like in everyday life.
w.j: John treats the Baptist as a witness. His whole role is to point to Jesus.

groups.sh: The Spirit comes down like a dove and a voice from heaven speaks.

m: The voice speaks about Jesus: "This is my beloved Son."
Only Matthew has John’s hesitation and Jesus’ answer about fulfilling all righteousness.
k: The voice speaks to Jesus: "You are my beloved Son."
l: The voice speaks to Jesus, and Luke notes that Jesus was praying.
j: Never describes the baptism itself. Reports what John the Baptist saw, and calls Jesus the Lamb of God.

w.m: The public declaration matches Matthew’s interest in Jesus’ identity being recognized, and his answer shows Jesus identifying with his people.
w.k: A private moment for Jesus in Mark, and the first time anyone in the story hears who he is.
w.l: Luke’s attention to prayer shows up here, and in the other places he notes Jesus praying.
w.j: In John the Baptist is the witness, so the story is told as his testimony.

groups.sh: The Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness, where he fasts and is tempted by Satan.

m: Three temptations; the last is on a high mountain.
Jesus answers each with Scripture from Deuteronomy.
k: Only two verses. Alone says he was "with the wild animals."
l: Three temptations in a different order; the last is at the temple in Jerusalem.
Jesus answers each with Deuteronomy. The devil leaves "until an opportune time."

w.m: The mountain as the climax fits Matthew’s mountain scenes (Sermon, transfiguration, final commission). Jesus succeeds where Israel failed in the wilderness.
w.k: Mark states the conflict and moves on; the real battle runs through the whole book.
w.l: Luke ends in Jerusalem, the city where his Gospel will climax, and notes that the devil left "until an opportune time."

groups.sh: After John is arrested, Jesus goes to Galilee and starts to preach.

m: Moves Jesus to Capernaum and quotes Isaiah about "Galilee of the Gentiles."
k: Gives his message in a line: the time is fulfilled, the kingdom is near, repent and believe.
l: Says only that he taught in the synagogues and was praised by all.

w.m: Matthew supplies the prophecy, because a Jewish reader would ask whether this fits the Scriptures.
w.k: Mark states Jesus’ message as a summary and gets to the action.
w.l: Luke saves the fuller opening for the next scene, at Nazareth.

groups.sh: Jesus calls fishermen, including Simon Peter and Andrew, to follow him.

m: Almost identical to Mark: Jesus walks by the sea and calls two sets of brothers, who leave nets and boat at once.
k: Almost identical to Matthew.
l: Puts the call after a large catch of fish. Peter falls at Jesus’ knees: "depart from me, for I am a sinful man."
j: Set earlier, in Judea: Andrew, a former follower of John the Baptist, brings his brother Simon, and Jesus gives him the name Cephas.

w.m: Matthew and Mark focus on the authority of Jesus’ call: he speaks, and they leave everything.
w.l: Luke tells how a man comes to follow: through a wonder, his own unworthiness and a promise of "catching people."
w.j: John shows that a first meeting with Jesus can come through someone else’s testimony ("we have found the Messiah").

groups.sh: Fishermen who caught nothing all night are told where to cast the net, and the catch is huge.

l: Placed at the beginning of the ministry. Jesus is in the boat.
j: Placed after the resurrection. Jesus stands on the shore and the disciples recognize him only after the catch.
Whether these are two events or one remembered in two settings is debated. The empty night and the surprising catch are the same.

w.l: Luke uses it as a call story: "from now on you will be catching people."
w.j: John uses it to restore Peter after his denial and to show the risen Jesus caring for his friends.

groups.sh: In his hometown Jesus teaches in the synagogue and the people take offense at him.

m: Placed later, much shorter. Ends quietly: "he did not do many miracles there because of their unbelief."
k: Placed later, much shorter. Adds that Jesus "could do no mighty work" there.
l: Placed at the very start and the longest: Jesus reads Isaiah 61, says "today this Scripture is fulfilled," and recalls how Elijah and Elisha helped outsiders. The crowd tries to throw him off a cliff.

w.l: Luke makes it Jesus’ opening statement: good news to the poor, and God’s mercy going to outsiders. This sets up the rest of the Gospel.
w.k: Mark shows the first signs of rejection, which grow through the book.
w.m: Matthew places it after the parables of the kingdom, as another example of a mixed reception.

groups.t: The man with an unclean spirit
groups.sh: On a Sabbath in Capernaum Jesus teaches with authority and casts out an unclean spirit.

k: The first miracle in Mark.
l: Very close to Mark. Adds that the demon threw the man down "without injuring him."

w.k: This is the first miracle in Mark, and it shows Jesus’ authority over evil.
w.l: Luke follows Mark closely here, with small changes in wording that make the scene smoother.

groups.sh: Jesus heals Simon’s mother-in-law of a fever and she serves them.

m: Mentions only Jesus entering Peter’s house. Jesus touches her hand.
k: Names Andrew, James and John as present.
l: Jesus "rebuked the fever."

w.m: Matthew trims the details and puts the healing in a series of ten miracles in chapters 8–9.
w.k: Mark keeps the eyewitness details (the four disciples, taking her by the hand).
w.l: Luke pictures the fever as a force Jesus commands, the way he speaks to demons.

groups.sh: At sunset the whole town brings sick and possessed people, and Jesus heals them.

m: Adds a quotation from Isaiah: "He took our infirmities and bore our diseases."
k: Jesus would not let the demons speak because they knew who he was.
l: Jesus lays his hands on each one. Like Mark, he would not let the demons speak.

w.m: The Isaiah quotation shows Jesus’ healings as the work of the Suffering Servant.
w.k: Mark’s "messianic secret" shows here: Jesus does not want the demons to reveal him.
w.l: Luke’s detail ("laying his hands on each one") shows personal care for each person.

groups.sh: Jesus goes through Galilee teaching, preaching and healing.

m: A summary of the whole region listening to him, from Syria to the Decapolis to Judea.
k: A moment alone in prayer before dawn; the crowds want to keep him.
l: The same quiet moment and the crowds who wanted him to stay.

w.m: Matthew sets this summary right before the Sermon on the Mount so that the crowds are in place for it.
w.k: Mark shows Jesus choosing his mission over popularity: "that is why I came out."
w.l: Luke has Jesus explain, "I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns."

groups.sh: A man with leprosy asks to be made clean, Jesus touches him, and tells him to show himself to the priest.

m: Placed right after the Sermon on the Mount. Does not mention the news spreading.
k: Jesus is moved with compassion (some manuscripts read "anger") and sternly sends the man away. The man spreads the news so widely that Jesus cannot enter towns openly.
l: Says the man was "full of leprosy."

w.m: Matthew shows Jesus respecting the Law (go to the priest) just after a sermon about fulfilling it.
w.k: Mark draws attention to Jesus’ emotions and to the tension between his fame and his mission.
w.l: Luke, a physician in tradition, gives the severity of the disease and adds Jesus’ habit of withdrawing to pray.

groups.t: The paralyzed man lowered through a roof
groups.sh: Jesus forgives a paralytic’s sins, and when scribes object, heals him to show his authority.

m: Leaves out the roof. Ends with the crowd praising God who gave "such authority to men."
k: Includes the friends removing the roof.
l: Includes the roof, and adds that Pharisees and teachers of the law had come from every village.

w.m: Matthew condenses it to focus on the question of Jesus’ authority to forgive sins.
w.k: Mark gives the vivid action: the crowd, the roof, the digging.
w.l: Luke widens the opposition (teachers from every village, even Jerusalem) and notes that "the power of the Lord was with him to heal."

groups.sh: Jesus calls a tax collector to follow him, then eats with tax collectors and sinners.

m: Calls him Matthew. Alone adds "I desire mercy, not sacrifice" (Hosea).
k: Calls him Levi.
l: Calls him Levi. Says he "left everything" and held a great feast, and adds "to repentance."

w.m: The author tells his own call story briefly, and the Hosea quotation again tells readers that mercy matters more than ritual.
w.l: Luke’s "to repentance" and his focus on the feast fit his theme of Jesus welcoming sinners.

groups.sh: Asked why his disciples do not fast, Jesus talks about the bridegroom, a patch and wineskins.

m: It is John’s disciples who ask.
k: People compare the disciples with those of John and the Pharisees.
l: Same as Mark, and ends with a line only Luke has: "no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, ‘The old is better.’"

w.m: Matthew shows a link with John’s own followers.
w.l: Luke’s last line recognizes why some people stay with what they know.

groups.sh: Hungry disciples pick grain on the Sabbath, and Jesus answers with David and the Son of Man being "Lord of the Sabbath."

m: Alone adds two arguments: priests work on the Sabbath in the temple, and "I desire mercy, not sacrifice."
k: Alone has "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath."
l: Adds that the disciples rubbed the grain in their hands.

w.m: Matthew builds a case from the Law itself to answer Jewish readers who valued Sabbath keeping.
w.k: Mark states the principle: the Sabbath is a gift for people.
w.l: Luke keeps it brief and close to Mark.

groups.t: The man with the withered hand
groups.sh: On a Sabbath Jesus heals a man’s hand in a synagogue, and his opponents begin to plot.

m: Jesus argues from a sheep fallen into a pit that it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.
k: Jesus looks around "with anger" and is grieved at their hardness of heart. The Pharisees plot with the Herodians.
l: Notes it was the right hand. The opponents discuss "what they might do to Jesus."

w.m: Matthew supplies an argument from everyday life that a Jewish listener would accept.
w.k: Mark shows Jesus’ emotions; the plot to kill him begins here.
w.l: Luke notes it was the right hand, and says Jesus asked the man to stand up in front of everyone.

groups.sh: Great crowds come from every direction for healing.

m: Jesus withdraws, and Matthew quotes the Servant Song of Isaiah 42.
k: Lists the regions: Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, Idumea, beyond the Jordan, Tyre and Sidon.
l: Sets the crowd on a level place, as the setting for the sermon that follows.

w.m: Isaiah 42 presents Jesus as the gentle Servant in whom the Gentiles will hope.
w.k: Mark shows the size of Jesus’ fame, which makes the plot against him more urgent.
w.l: Luke connects it directly to the Sermon on the Plain.

groups.sh: Jesus names twelve apostles, and the lists agree on all but one name.

m: Lists them in pairs and notes that Matthew is "the tax collector." Calls one of them Thaddaeus.
k: Says he appointed them "that they might be with him" and be sent out. Also has Thaddaeus.
l: Jesus spends the night in prayer on the mountain first. Lists "Judas son of James" where Matthew and Mark have Thaddaeus.

w.m: Matthew puts the list at the start of his mission discourse.
w.k: Mark puts being "with him" first, then being sent.
w.l: Luke prefaces the choice with a night of prayer.

groups.sh: Jesus blesses the poor, the hungry, the mourning and the persecuted.

m: Eight or nine blessings, in the third person ("Blessed are the poor in spirit").
"Poor in spirit," "hunger and thirst for righteousness." Given on a mountain.
l: Four blessings and four matching woes, in the second person ("Blessed are you who are poor").
Simply "poor" and "hungry now." Given on a level place.

w.m: Matthew spiritualizes the conditions: the blessing is for those humble before God. The mountain echoes Moses at Sinai.
w.l: Luke stresses the reversal of fortunes, with woes to the rich. This matches his concern for the poor throughout.

groups.sh: Love your enemies, bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you.

m: Framed against "an eye for an eye." Ends "Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect."
Has "greet only your brothers."
l: Ends "Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful."
Has "if you do good to those who do good to you" and "if you lend to those from whom you expect to receive."

w.m: Matthew sets it against the Law as the fuller meaning ("You have heard that it was said...").
w.l: Luke asks how a believer treats outsiders, and gives mercy as the pattern.

groups.sh: Do not judge so you will not be judged; remove the log from your own eye first.

m: Shorter: one warning inside the Sermon.
l: Adds "forgive and you will be forgiven" and "give, and it will be given to you," with a full measure poured into the lap, and the blind leading the blind.

w.m: Matthew keeps the saying short, a single warning inside the Sermon.
w.l: Luke links it to generosity and forgiveness, the themes of his sermon.

groups.sh: A good tree bears good fruit, and a bad tree bad fruit.

m: Applies it to false prophets "in sheep’s clothing." Repeats the tree saying at 12:33–35.
l: Applies it to what comes out of the heart through the mouth.

w.m: Matthew warns his community about teachers who sound right but live wrongly.
w.l: Luke makes it about speech and the heart: "out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks."

groups.t: Hearing and doing: the house on the rock
groups.sh: Whoever hears and does Jesus’ words is like a man who builds on rock.

m: Starts with "Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord." Builders on rock and on sand. The crowds are astonished.
l: Starts with "Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and not do what I tell you?" Digging deep to the rock versus building without a foundation.

w.m: Matthew ends the Sermon with a verdict about authority: Jesus teaches "not as their scribes."
w.l: Luke speaks directly to people who already call Jesus Lord.

groups.sh: Jesus teaches his disciples to pray to the Father, for his name, his kingdom, daily bread and forgiveness.

m: Longer: "Our Father in heaven," "your will be done on earth," "deliver us from the evil one." "Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors."
Placed in the Sermon on the Mount, as a contrast to showy prayer.
l: Shorter, begins "Father." "Forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us."
Given in answer to a disciple’s request after watching Jesus pray.

w.m: A pattern to replace showy prayer, suited to the shared prayer of a community.
w.l: The prayer grows out of Jesus’ own praying, and Luke follows it with parables about persistence.

groups.sh: Ask and it will be given; if earthly fathers give good gifts, how much more will your Father?

m: The Father will "give good things to those who ask him." Examples: bread and a stone, a fish and a snake.
l: The Father will "give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him." Examples: a fish and a serpent, an egg and a scorpion.

w.m: Matthew puts the saying in a general promise: good things.
w.l: Luke names the gift: the Holy Spirit, a theme in his Gospel and in Acts.

groups.sh: Look at the birds and the lilies; your Father knows what you need.

m: "Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness." Points to "the birds of the air."
l: "Seek his kingdom." Points to "the ravens," which neither sow nor reap.
Adds "Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom" and "sell your possessions and give to the needy."

w.m: Matthew sets it inside the Sermon, as a contrast to a divided heart ("You cannot serve God and money").
w.l: Luke follows it with the parable of the rich fool and turns it into a call to give.

groups.sh: No one can serve two masters; you cannot serve God and money.

m: "No one can serve two masters."
l: "No servant can serve two masters." Otherwise almost word for word.

w.m: In Matthew it prepares the teaching on anxiety.
w.l: In Luke it ends the parable of the dishonest manager.

groups.t: The narrow gate and the narrow door
groups.sh: The way into the kingdom is narrow and few find it.

m: Two gates and two roads, narrow and wide.
l: A closed door where people knock and hear "I do not know where you come from," and then many come from east and west to the feast.

w.m: Matthew presents a choice between two ways, as at the end of the Sermon.
w.l: Luke makes it about being left out, and about people from every direction being welcomed.

groups.sh: A man with authority asks Jesus to heal a servant or son at a distance, and Jesus does so by a word.

m: The centurion comes to Jesus himself. Adds that many will come from east and west to the feast.
l: He sends Jewish elders and then friends, saying he is not worthy to have Jesus under his roof.
j: A similar story about a royal official whose son is dying, in Cana. Many think it is a different event; others see a retelling.

w.m: Matthew uses the Gentile’s faith to point to the wider welcome to come.
w.l: Luke stresses the man’s humility and goodness to the Jewish community ("he loves our nation").
w.j: John gives a "sign" that leads the whole household to faith.

groups.sh: Foxes have holes, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head; let the dead bury their own dead.

m: The first man is a scribe and the second "another of the disciples." Two would-be followers.
l: Adds a third who wants to say goodbye to family first, and Jesus replies about putting a hand to the plow.

w.m: Matthew puts it before the boat and storm, as a test of discipleship.
w.l: Luke places it as Jesus sets out for Jerusalem, where the cost is greatest.

groups.sh: Jesus gives the Twelve authority over unclean spirits and sends them out to preach and heal with little to carry.

m: No staff and no sandals. Adds "Go nowhere among the Gentiles or Samaritans, but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel," and a long instruction that continues with persecution.
k: They may take a staff and sandals, but no bread, bag or money. Sent two by two; they anoint the sick with oil.
l: No staff, bag, bread or money. Short, and linked to Herod’s question about who Jesus is.

w.m: Matthew shapes the mission around Israel first and builds a discourse on what discipleship costs.
w.k: Mark sends them two by two and says they anointed the sick with oil.
w.l: Luke ties this mission to Herod’s question about who Jesus is.

groups.sh: The harvest is plentiful, the workers few; go as lambs among wolves, eat what you are given, and say "the kingdom of God has come near."

m: The same words appear inside the Twelve’s commission.
l: Only Luke has a second, larger sending of seventy(-two) disciples.

w.m: Matthew gathers the sayings in one mission speech.
w.l: Luke has two missions, perhaps foreshadowing the mission to the whole world in Acts.

groups.sh: Chorazin and Bethsaida would have repented long ago; Capernaum will be brought down.

m: Ends with a comparison to Sodom. The woes come after the Twelve have been sent out.
l: Nearly identical wording. The woes come after the seventy-two are sent; the Sodom saying is earlier, at 10:12.

w.m: Matthew places it after John’s question and before the invitation to the weary.
w.l: Luke places it right after the sending of the seventy-two, as the cost of rejecting the messengers.

groups.t: "Come to me": revealed to little ones
groups.sh: Jesus thanks the Father for revealing these things to little children, and says no one knows the Son except the Father.

m: Continues with "Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden."
l: Jesus rejoices "in the Holy Spirit." Follows with "blessed are the eyes that see what you see," which Matthew has at 13:16–17.

w.m: Matthew ends with the gentle invitation and the "easy yoke."
w.l: Luke ties it to the return of the seventy-two and to the joy of the Spirit.

groups.sh: John, in prison, sends to ask "Are you the one who is to come?" and Jesus answers by pointing to what is happening.

m: Jesus answers by pointing to what is happening.
l: Jesus first heals many people in front of John’s messengers. Adds that tax collectors "justified God."

w.m: In Matthew the answer helps readers understand why Jesus’ ministry looks different from what many expected.
w.l: Luke makes the proof visible (healings in front of the messengers), and adds that tax collectors "justified God."

groups.sh: Opponents say Jesus casts out demons by the prince of demons; Jesus replies that a house divided cannot stand.

m: Starts with the healing of a mute man. "By the Spirit of God." Continues to the unforgivable sin against the Holy Spirit.
k: Surrounds the scene with the family’s worry ("he is out of his mind") and scribes from Jerusalem. Continues to the unforgivable sin.
l: Starts with the healing of a mute man. "By the finger of God."

w.m: Matthew follows it with warnings that words reveal the heart (12:33–37).
w.k: Mark frames it with the family’s misunderstanding, to show that even those close to Jesus struggled.
w.l: Luke’s "finger of God" recalls the Exodus, so that the kingdom is a new act of rescue.

groups.sh: An evil generation asks for a sign, and no sign will be given except the sign of Jonah.

m: Explains the sign: "three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish," pointing to Jesus’ death and resurrection.
Adds that the Queen of the South and the men of Nineveh will rise up and condemn this generation.
k: Shortest: "no sign will be given to this generation." Jesus sighs deeply, then leaves.
l: Jonah was a sign to the people of Nineveh, as the Son of Man will be to this generation.
Like Matthew, adds the Queen of the South and the men of Nineveh.

w.m: Matthew connects the sign explicitly to burial and resurrection.
w.k: Mark has Jesus sigh deeply, then leave.
w.l: Luke focuses on preaching and repentance: the Ninevites repented at Jonah’s preaching, and "something greater than Jonah is here."

groups.sh: When his family is outside, Jesus says those who do God’s will are his mother and brothers.

m: Jesus points to his disciples.
k: Jesus looks at those sitting around him.
l: Jesus says "those who hear the word of God and do it."

w.m: Matthew points to the disciples as the new family.
w.k: Mark sets it after the family’s earlier worry (3:21), which sharpens the contrast.
w.l: Luke puts the emphasis on hearing and doing the word.

groups.t: The lamp and what is hidden
groups.sh: A lamp is put on a stand, not under a basket.

m: About the disciples’ good works: "you are the light of the world."
k: The lamp stands for hidden things coming to light, and for how you listen.
l: Same as Mark: "pay attention to how you hear." Repeats the lamp saying at 11:33.

w.m: Matthew applies it to the disciples’ visible lives.
w.k: Mark links it to the parable of the sower: the message is meant to be revealed.
w.l: Luke stresses attentive listening.

groups.sh: A sower scatters seed on four kinds of soil, and only the good soil bears fruit.

m: Yields of hundredfold, sixtyfold and thirtyfold.
k: Yields of thirty, sixty and a hundred.
l: A single yield, a hundredfold. The seed on the path is trampled on, and the seed on rock "withered for lack of moisture."

w.m: Matthew starts a chapter of seven parables about the kingdom.
w.k: Mark opens with "Listen!" and presents it as the key to understanding all parables (4:13).
w.l: Luke trims the details and goes on to the lamp and Jesus’ true family.

groups.sh: To outsiders it is given in parables so that seeing they may not see, quoting Isaiah 6.

m: The longest version. Says "because" seeing they do not see, quotes Isaiah at length, and adds a blessing on the disciples’ eyes and ears.
k: Says "so that" they may not understand.
l: The shortest version.

w.m: Matthew states that people are judged by how they respond: it is a fulfillment of Isaiah.
w.k: Mark’s wording makes the parables themselves a mystery to those outside.
w.l: Luke is brief and moves on to the explanation.

groups.sh: The seed is the word; the soils are the ways people receive it.

m: Ties understanding to bearing fruit.
k: Opens with "Do you not understand this parable? How will you understand all the parables?"
l: Calls the seed "the word of God" and the good soil "an honest and good heart." The seed on the path is taken "lest they believe and be saved."

w.m: Matthew ties understanding to bearing fruit.
w.k: Mark exposes the disciples’ slowness.
w.l: Luke focuses on belief and salvation.

groups.sh: The kingdom starts as small as a mustard seed and grows large.

m: Pairs the mustard seed with the leaven. The man sows it in "his field."
k: Only the mustard seed, which becomes "the greatest of all shrubs."
l: Pairs it with the leaven. The man puts it "in his garden."

w.m: Matthew pairs the two to show the kingdom’s surprising growth from a small start.
w.k: Mark places it within the series of seed parables.
w.l: Luke pairs a man’s parable with a woman’s, a pattern in his Gospel.

groups.sh: Better to be thrown into the sea than to cause a little one to stumble; salt is good.

m: Hand, foot and eye. Salt is at 5:13.
k: The longest version: "it is better to enter life crippled" three times (hand, foot, eye), and salt.
l: Only the millstone (17:1–2), and salt separately (14:34–35).

w.m: Matthew places it in a discourse on life in the community.
w.k: Mark makes it a sharp call to cut off what leads to sin.
w.l: Luke makes it a short warning about those who lead others astray.

groups.sh: A sudden storm threatens the boat; Jesus rebukes the wind and sea and there is a great calm.

m: "Lord, save us!" Jesus rebukes their little faith before calming the storm.
k: Jesus asleep on a cushion; "do you not care that we are perishing?" He says "Peace! Be still!" and then "Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?"
l: "Master, Master, we are perishing!" He calms the storm and then asks "Where is your faith?"

w.m: Matthew presents the disciples as people of "little faith" and has them call him "Lord," a title of worship.
w.k: Mark keeps the eyewitness details (the cushion, the other boats) and blunt questions from the disciples.
w.l: Luke softens the disciples’ words and keeps the focus on the wonder and on who Jesus is.

groups.sh: Jesus crosses to the other side, meets a man (or men) with demons, sends them into pigs, and the herd rushes into the sea.

m: Two men, in the country of the Gadarenes. A short account.
Interpreters differ on why Matthew has two: some think Mark and Luke focus on the more prominent man.
k: One man, in the country of the Gerasenes. A much longer account, including the name "Legion," the man’s request to follow Jesus, and his proclaiming in the Decapolis.
l: One man, much like Mark, who proclaims throughout the whole city.

w.m: Matthew trims the story to its central point, Jesus’ authority over evil forces.
w.k: Mark spends the most time on the man’s condition and healing: he becomes the first missionary to the Gentile region.
w.l: Luke includes the sense of a man restored: sitting, clothed and in his right mind, at Jesus’ feet.

groups.t: Jairus’ daughter and the woman who touched Jesus
groups.sh: A synagogue leader begs Jesus to heal his daughter; on the way a woman with a long illness touches Jesus’ cloak, and then Jesus raises the girl.

m: The leader says his daughter "has just died." The whole story is quick.
k: She is dying when he comes, and dies on the way. The woman "suffered much under many physicians." Jesus asks "Who touched me?" Gives the Aramaic "Talitha cumi."
l: Like Mark, with the question "Who touched me?" Says no one could heal the woman (the "physicians" detail is missing in some manuscripts). The girl is an only daughter.

w.m: Matthew keeps the two healings short and focuses on faith and power over death.
w.k: Mark’s detail and his sandwiched structure show faith under pressure.
w.l: Luke stresses that the girl was an only daughter, about twelve years old.

groups.t: Herod and the death of John
groups.sh: Herod hears of Jesus and wonders whether he is John risen from the dead.

m: Tells the story of Herod’s banquet, Herodias’ daughter and John’s beheading as a flashback.
k: The same flashback, told most fully.
l: Only Herod’s puzzlement: "John I beheaded; but who is this?"

w.m: Matthew shows John’s fate as a hint of what awaits Jesus.
w.k: Mark places it right between the sending and the return of the Twelve, and shows that a king can fear a prophet and still kill him.
w.l: Luke keeps the focus on the question of who Jesus is, which leads to Peter’s confession.

groups.sh: Jesus takes five loaves and two fish, gives thanks, and feeds a great crowd, with twelve baskets left over.

m: Counts five thousand men "besides women and children."
k: The people sit in groups of hundreds and fifties on "green grass."
l: Groups of about fifty.
j: Jesus asks Philip "where are we to buy bread?" to test him. Andrew finds a boy with barley loaves. The crowd wants to make him king. Set near Passover.

w.m: Matthew notes the count was five thousand men "besides women and children."
w.k: Mark begins with Jesus seeing the crowd "like sheep without a shepherd."
w.l: Luke sets it in Bethsaida after the Twelve return from their mission.
w.j: John uses it as the opening to the bread of life teaching: Jesus himself is the bread.

groups.sh: The disciples row against the wind at night and Jesus comes to them walking on the water; "It is I; do not be afraid."

m: Only Matthew has Peter step out onto the water and begin to sink. The disciples worship: "Truly you are the Son of God."
k: Jesus "meant to pass by them." The disciples’ "hearts were hardened."
j: The boat immediately reaches the shore. Luke has no version of this story.

w.m: Matthew turns the scene into a lesson on doubt and faith, with Peter as an example.
w.k: Mark ties it to the disciples’ failure to understand the loaves.
w.j: John keeps it short, as a "sign" of who Jesus is. His "It is I" is "I am" in Greek, words John uses elsewhere for Jesus’ identity.

groups.sh: Pharisees object that the disciples eat with unwashed hands; Jesus says what comes out of a person defiles, not what goes in.

m: Leaves out the explanations of customs. Ends with "To eat with unwashed hands does not defile."
k: Explains Jewish customs for his readers (washing hands, cups, pots) and adds "Thus he declared all foods clean."

w.m: Matthew’s Jewish readers did not need purity customs explained, so he says "unwashed hands" and no more.
w.k: Mark explains the customs for a mixed audience and draws the conclusion about all foods.

groups.sh: A Gentile woman asks Jesus to heal her daughter, and answers his remark about "the children’s bread" with faith.

m: Calls her a "Canaanite," who cries "Lord, Son of David." The disciples urge Jesus to send her away, and he says "I was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel."
k: Calls her "a Greek, a Syrophoenician by birth." Jesus says "Let the children be fed first."

w.m: Matthew reflects the tension between Israel’s priority and the Gentiles’ faith.
w.k: Mark’s "first" leaves the door open to the Gentiles right away.

groups.sh: Jesus feeds a crowd with seven loaves and a few fish and seven baskets are left over.

m: A separate event from the five thousand; Jesus refers to both at 16:9–10. Counts four thousand men "besides women and children."
k: Close to Matthew. Jesus also refers to both feedings (8:19–20). The baskets are a larger kind than at the five thousand.

w.m: Matthew mentions "four thousand men besides women and children," as with the five thousand.
w.k: Mark puts it among Gentile areas (the Decapolis), which many take as a sign that Jesus feeds Gentiles too.

groups.sh: Jesus warns about the yeast of the Pharisees and the disciples think he is talking about bread.

m: Explains that the yeast was the Pharisees’ and Sadducees’ teaching, and the disciples understand.
k: Mentions the "leaven of Herod" and ends with a series of questions: "Do you not yet understand?"

w.m: Matthew shows the disciples finally understanding.
w.k: Mark leaves the disciples puzzled, which is the point: they do not see yet.

groups.sh: Jesus asks who people say he is, and Peter answers.

m: Peter says "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Only Matthew has Jesus’ reply about the rock and the keys of the kingdom.
k: Peter says "You are the Christ."
l: Peter says "The Christ of God." Jesus was praying alone.
j: Set when many disciples leave: "You have the words of eternal life... you are the Holy One of God."

w.m: Matthew shows Peter’s role in the community and the authority of the church to bind and loose.
w.k: Mark has Jesus tell them to keep it quiet; the confession is the center of the Gospel.
w.l: Luke puts it in a context of prayer.
w.j: John’s version is set after the crowds drift away, so it is a confession of loyalty.

groups.t: The first prediction of the passion
groups.sh: Jesus says he must suffer, be killed and be raised on the third day.

m: Says Jesus "must go to Jerusalem." Peter rebukes him and Jesus calls him "Satan."
k: Jesus speaks "plainly." Peter rebukes him and Jesus calls him "Satan."
l: Leaves out the exchange with Peter.

w.m: Matthew shows Peter’s failure right after his success, and warns about mistaking God’s plan.
w.k: Mark says Jesus spoke this "plainly."
w.l: Luke gives the prediction without the rebuke, probably to keep Peter’s role in view for Acts.

groups.sh: Whoever wants to follow Jesus must deny himself, take up his cross and follow; whoever loses his life for Jesus’ sake will find it.

m: Some standing there will see "the Son of Man coming in his kingdom." Adds that he will "repay each person according to what he has done."
k: "For my sake and the gospel’s." Some will see "the kingdom of God come with power."
l: "Take up his cross daily." Some will see "the kingdom of God."

w.m: Matthew adds judgment: each will be repaid for what he has done.
w.k: Mark adds "and the gospel," the good news about Jesus.
w.l: Luke makes discipleship an everyday matter: "daily."

groups.sh: Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a mountain, is transfigured, and a voice says "This is my beloved Son."

m: His face shone like the sun, and the disciples fell on their faces.
k: His clothes became "such as no one on earth could bleach them."
l: "About eight days" after the sayings, and Jesus went up to pray. Moses and Elijah speak with him about his "exodus" at Jerusalem. The disciples were heavy with sleep.

w.m: Matthew highlights the shining face and the voice, with a link to Moses at Sinai.
w.k: Mark stresses the disciples’ fear and confusion, and the command not to tell until the resurrection.
w.l: Luke makes the topic of conversation Jesus’ coming death in Jerusalem.

groups.t: The boy with an unclean spirit
groups.sh: At the foot of the mountain a father brings his son, and the disciples have been unable to cast the spirit out.

m: The boy "has seizures." Adds that "faith like a grain of mustard seed" can move mountains.
k: The longest and most vivid, including the father’s cry "I believe; help my unbelief!" and the convulsions.
l: The boy is an only child. Ends with all astonished at "the majesty of God."

w.m: Matthew turns it into a lesson about little faith.
w.k: Mark gives the human drama: a father, a struggling faith.
w.l: Luke ends with "all were astonished at the majesty of God."

groups.sh: Jesus says the Son of Man will be delivered into human hands and killed, and the disciples do not understand.

m: The disciples were "greatly distressed."
k: They did not understand and were afraid to ask.
l: The same, and adds that the meaning was "concealed from them."

w.m: Matthew shows their sorrow.
w.k: Mark shows their fear.
w.l: Luke says it was hidden, which points to a later insight.

groups.sh: The disciples argue about who is greatest, and Jesus sets a child in their midst.

m: The disciples ask Jesus. "Unless you turn and become like children."
k: Jesus asks what they were arguing about on the road, and they are silent. "If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all."
l: "The one who is least among you all is the one who is great."

w.m: Matthew starts a discourse on community life with humility as its foundation.
w.k: Mark shows the disciples caught in the act.
w.l: Luke says "the one who is least among you all is the one who is great."

groups.t: Someone casting out demons in Jesus’ name
groups.sh: "Whoever is not against us is for us."

k: Adds a cup of water given in Jesus’ name. Matthew has no parallel here, but at 12:30 he has the opposite wording: "whoever is not with me is against me."
l: Ends with the saying "Whoever is not against you is for you."

w.k: Mark balances the saying with a promise for anyone who helps Jesus’ followers.
w.l: Luke shows the disciples’ narrow attitude, just before they want to call down fire on a Samaritan village.

groups.sh: A shepherd leaves ninety-nine sheep to look for one that is lost and rejoices when he finds it.

m: The sheep "has gone astray," and the Father does not want "one of these little ones" to perish.
l: The shepherd carries the sheep home on his shoulders and calls his friends to rejoice; there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.

w.m: Matthew applies it to caring for a member of the community who has strayed.
w.l: Luke tells it to Pharisees who complain Jesus eats with sinners, and pairs it with the lost coin and the lost son.

groups.sh: Forgive a brother who repents, even many times.

m: "Seventy-seven times" (or seventy times seven).
l: "Seven times in a day."

w.m: Matthew sets it in a discourse on discipline and forgiveness in the community.
w.l: Luke places it right after the warning about stumbling blocks.

groups.sh: Do not fear those who kill the body; whoever acknowledges Jesus before others, he will acknowledge before his Father.

m: "I will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven." Has the sparrows and the hairs of your head.
l: "Before the angels of God." Also has the sparrows and the hairs of your head.

w.m: Matthew places it in the mission speech, as encouragement for those who will be persecuted.
w.l: Luke places it among warnings about hypocrisy and the coming judgment.

groups.sh: Jesus did not come to bring peace but division, even within families.

m: "I have not come to bring peace, but a sword."
l: "No, but rather division." Adds a line about a baptism he must undergo, and how distressed he is until it is accomplished.

w.m: Matthew speaks of a "sword," in a mission speech.
w.l: Luke ties it to Jesus’ own coming suffering, the "baptism" ahead.

groups.sh: A servant is put in charge, and a master returns at an unexpected time; the faithful one is rewarded and the unfaithful punished.

m: Ends with "weeping and gnashing of teeth."
l: Begins with Peter’s question "Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all?" Adds "everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required."

w.m: Matthew puts it inside the Olivet discourse as part of the call to be ready.
w.l: Luke makes it a lesson for leaders, with responsibility growing with what you are given.

groups.sh: "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem... how often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood."

m: Ends the woes against the scribes and Pharisees, spoken in the temple.
l: Spoken on the road to Jerusalem, after a warning that Herod wants to kill Jesus. The wording is almost the same.

w.m: Matthew puts it at the climax of Jesus’ public teaching, just before the final discourse.
w.l: Luke places it in the middle of the journey, so that Jerusalem is the destination from the start.

groups.t: The great banquet and the wedding feast
groups.sh: A host invites guests who refuse, so he invites others from the streets.

m: A king gives a wedding feast for his son. The guests mistreat and kill the servants, and the king burns their city. A man without a wedding garment is thrown out.
l: "A man" gives a "great banquet." The guests make excuses, and the servants bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame, and then people from the highways.

w.m: Matthew turns it into a parable about the kingdom, rejection of its messengers and the need for a response from those who accept.
w.l: Luke tells it at a Pharisee’s dinner and makes it about whom God invites: the poor, and outsiders.

groups.sh: A master entrusts money to servants, returns, and rewards those who used it and punishes the one who did not.

m: Three servants with five, two and one talents, given "according to ability."
l: Ten servants each given one mina, and a noble who goes to receive a kingdom, with citizens who say "We do not want this man to reign over us." The reward is ten or five cities.

w.m: Matthew puts it in the last teaching before the passion, a call to use what you have been given until the master returns.
w.l: Luke tells it as Jesus nears Jerusalem to correct the idea that the kingdom would appear immediately.

groups.t: Days of Noah and the coming of the Son of Man
groups.sh: As in the days of Noah, people go on eating and drinking until the flood comes; one will be taken and one left.

m: Two men in the field and two women grinding.
l: Adds the days of Lot and "Remember Lot’s wife," two in one bed, and ends with "Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather."

w.m: Matthew puts it in the Olivet discourse.
w.l: Luke places it in an earlier teaching about the day of the Son of Man.

groups.sh: Jesus teaches that what God has joined together, man must not separate, and calls remarriage after divorce adultery.

m: The Pharisees ask "Is it lawful to divorce one’s wife for any cause?" Jesus gives an exception for sexual immorality (19:9; also 5:32). Adds a conversation about eunuchs.
k: No exception. Says the same applies to a woman who divorces her husband.
l: Only a one-sentence saying.

w.m: Matthew joins a lively contemporary debate among Jewish teachers about the grounds for divorce, so his version names the exception.
w.k: Mark includes the case of a woman divorcing her husband, which many think reflects Roman law, where either spouse could start a divorce.
w.l: Luke gives the saying in a short form among teaching on money and the law.

groups.sh: "Let the little children come to me... for to such belongs the kingdom of God."

m: Jesus lays his hands on them and prays.
k: Jesus is "indignant" with the disciples and takes the children in his arms and blesses them.
l: People were bringing even infants.

w.m: Matthew keeps it short, as a scene of blessing.
w.k: Mark shows Jesus’ emotions and affection.
w.l: Luke’s "even infants" widens the picture of who may come.

groups.sh: A rich man asks what to do to inherit eternal life; Jesus tells him to sell what he has and follow, and he goes away sad.

m: He is a "young man." Asks "what good deed must I do?" and Jesus says "Why do you ask me about what is good?" Adds "If you would be perfect," and the promise that the apostles will sit on twelve thrones.
k: The man runs up and kneels, and Jesus "looked at him and loved him." "Good Teacher" ... "Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone."
l: Calls him a "ruler." "Good Teacher," with the same reply as Mark.

w.m: Matthew shifts the focus from Jesus’ goodness to the commandments and to "what is good," in the style of a rabbinic dispute.
w.k: Mark’s personal detail shows the cost of the call: Jesus loved him and still asked for everything.
w.l: Luke calls him a ruler, which fits his attention to wealth and power.

groups.sh: On the way to Jerusalem Jesus says he will be handed over, mocked, killed and raised.

m: Names crucifixion.
k: Has the most detail about the abuse: "mock him and spit on him and flog him."
l: These things are written by the prophets, and their meaning was hidden from the disciples.

w.m: Matthew is the first of the three to name crucifixion.
w.k: Mark has the most detail about the abuse.
w.l: Luke stresses fulfillment of Scripture.

groups.t: The request of James and John
groups.sh: "Whoever would be great among you must be your servant... the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many."

m: Their mother makes the request for them.
k: James and John make the request themselves.
l: No request. The dispute comes at the Last Supper, where Jesus adds "I am among you as the one who serves."

w.m: Matthew has the mother come with her sons, and the brothers answer Jesus themselves.
w.k: Mark states the ambition directly and moves to the "ransom."
w.l: Luke puts it at the supper, where Jesus gives the example of serving at table.

groups.sh: Blind men by the road cry out "Son of David, have mercy," and Jesus restores their sight.

m: Two blind men, as Jesus leaves Jericho. Jesus touches their eyes.
k: One man, named Bartimaeus, as Jesus leaves Jericho. Jesus says "Call him." The man throws off his cloak.
l: One man, "as he drew near to Jericho." The crowd rebukes him. The people give praise to God.

w.m: Matthew again has two men, with Jesus touching their eyes.
w.k: Mark remembers the name and the thrown-off cloak, and has the man follow Jesus "on the way."
w.l: Luke ends with the people giving praise to God.

groups.sh: Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a colt while crowds shout "Hosanna" and "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord."

m: A donkey and a colt, and a quotation from Zechariah 9.
k: A colt that no one has ridden. Ends quietly, with Jesus looking around the temple and leaving.
l: A colt that no one has ridden. The crowd shouts "Blessed is the King who comes"; the Pharisees want the disciples silenced and Jesus says "the stones will cry out." Alone adds Jesus weeping over Jerusalem (19:41–44).
j: The crowd had heard about the raising of Lazarus. The disciples understood the Zechariah quotation only later. The Pharisees say "the world has gone after him."

w.m: Matthew shows Jesus fulfilling Zechariah’s prophecy of a humble king.
w.k: Mark lets the entry end quietly, with Jesus looking around the temple and leaving.
w.l: Luke stresses peace in heaven and the grief of the king over the city that will reject him.
w.j: John connects the crowd to Lazarus and has the Pharisees say "the world has gone after him."

groups.sh: Jesus curses a fig tree that has no fruit and it withers; he tells the disciples about faith and prayer.

m: The tree withers at once, and the disciples are amazed.
k: Wraps the cursing around the cleansing of the temple (an "intercalation"). Notes "it was not the season for figs."

w.m: Matthew compresses it, concentrating on the lesson about faith.
w.k: Mark lets the fig tree comment on the temple: fruitless religion under judgment.

groups.sh: Jesus drives merchants and money changers out of the temple.

m: Placed in the last week. Adds that the blind and lame came to him and children cried Hosanna.
k: Placed in the last week. Alone says Jesus would not let anyone carry anything through the temple, and quotes "a house of prayer for all the nations."
l: Placed in the last week and short. The leaders seek to destroy him, but the people hang on his words.
j: Placed at the beginning of the ministry, at the first Passover (some take it as a second cleansing). Only John has the whip of cords, the sheep and oxen, and "destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up."

w.m: Matthew shows healing in the temple and children praising.
w.k: Mark’s "for all nations" is a pointed word for the Gentile court that was being used as a market.
w.l: Luke is short, ending with the leaders seeking to destroy him and the people hanging on his words.
w.j: John uses it as a sign of the temple’s replacement: Jesus’ own body.

groups.sh: Jesus is asked by what authority he acts and answers with a question about John’s baptism.

m: Asked by "chief priests and elders."
k: Asked by "chief priests, scribes and elders."
l: Asked by "chief priests and scribes with the elders." The leaders reason that the people would stone them. The rest is nearly identical.

w.m: Matthew follows with three parables aimed at the leaders.
w.k: Mark keeps it as one of a series of conflict stories in the temple.
w.l: Luke notes the people’s support for John and that the leaders fear them.

groups.sh: A landowner sends servants to tenants who beat and kill them, then sends his son, whom they kill. "The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone."

m: The son is thrown out and killed. The leaders themselves answer how the owner will deal with the tenants. Adds "the kingdom of God will be taken away from you."
k: The son is killed and thrown out of the vineyard.
l: The son is thrown out and killed. The hearers say "Surely not!"

w.m: Matthew makes the parable a judgment on the leaders and a promise to a people who bear fruit.
w.k: Mark and Matthew both build the opening on the vineyard song of Isaiah 5.
w.l: Luke adds the reaction "May it never be!" and the saying that everyone who falls on the stone will be broken.

groups.sh: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s."

m: Pharisees and Herodians question him.
k: Pharisees and Herodians question him.
l: The leaders send "spies who pretended to be sincere," and the specific accusation is that Jesus forbids paying taxes.

w.m: Matthew stresses the Pharisees’ plot.
w.k: Mark highlights the trap.
w.l: Luke ties it to the later charge before Pilate (23:2), "forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar."

groups.sh: Sadducees ask whose wife a woman will be in the resurrection after seven brothers; Jesus says the dead are raised and God is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

m: Ends with the crowd astonished at his teaching.
k: Jesus says "you are quite wrong" at the end.
l: Adds "the sons of this age marry... but those who are considered worthy to attain to that age... are equal to angels." Ends with scribes saying "Teacher, you have spoken well."

w.m: Matthew shows the crowds as amazed.
w.k: Mark has Jesus say "you are quite wrong" at the end.
w.l: Luke adds teaching on the nature of the age to come.

groups.sh: Love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself.

m: A lawyer tests him. Jesus says "On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets."
k: The longest: a friendly scribe asks, Jesus gives the Shema (Deuteronomy 6) and Leviticus 19, the scribe agrees that this is more than sacrifices, and Jesus says "You are not far from the kingdom of God."
l: The lawyer himself gives the two commandments, in answer to his question about eternal life, and it leads to the parable of the Good Samaritan.

w.m: Matthew shows Jesus giving the Law’s center in an argument with opponents.
w.k: Mark shows a scribe who agrees, one of the few friendly exchanges with a leader.
w.l: Luke uses it to launch the question "Who is my neighbor?"

groups.sh: Jesus asks how David can call the Christ "Lord" if he is David’s son (Psalm 110).

m: The Pharisees answer "the son of David." No one dared question him again.
k: Jesus asks while teaching in the temple, and the great throng heard him gladly.
l: Very close to Mark.

w.m: Matthew ends the series of questions with Jesus’ own question.
w.k: Mark has the crowd delighted.
w.l: Luke is very close to Mark.

groups.t: Warnings about the scribes and Pharisees
groups.sh: Beware of those who love the best seats and long robes and who devour widows’ houses.

m: A full chapter with seven "woes" and rebukes about hypocrisy.
k: Three verses.
l: Three verses. A longer set of woes is elsewhere, at a Pharisee’s table (11:37–54).

w.m: Matthew sets up a sustained confrontation, and exhorts the disciples not to be called "rabbi."
w.k: Mark keeps it as a brief warning, followed directly by the widow’s offering.
w.l: Luke keeps the short warning in the temple and uses the longer one in another setting.

groups.sh: A poor widow gives two small coins and Jesus says she has put in more than all the others.

k: Nearly identical to Luke. Alone explains the coins ("a penny"). Matthew does not have this story.
l: Nearly identical to Mark.

w.k: Mark puts it after the warning about devouring widows, as a picture of the opposite.
w.l: Luke uses it to show true giving, from need rather than from abundance.

groups.t: The temple’s fall and the signs
groups.sh: Jesus says not one stone will be left on another, and warns of wars, earthquakes, persecution and false messiahs.

m: Set on the Mount of Olives, with the disciples asking privately. The gospel will be "proclaimed throughout the whole world."
k: Set on the Mount of Olives, with Peter, James, John and Andrew asking.
l: Set in the temple, with "some" speaking. Adds "dreadful portents and great signs from heaven" and the promise "I will give you a mouth and wisdom."

w.m: Matthew presents the signs as the beginning of birth pains.
w.k: Mark urges the readers to "be on guard."
w.l: Luke includes the cost of witness and the promise of help for those on trial.

groups.t: The abomination and the fall of Jerusalem
groups.sh: Those in Judea must flee to the mountains; there will be great distress.

m: Speaks of the "abomination of desolation" (Daniel), with "let the reader understand."
k: The same, with "let the reader understand."
l: Says "when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies" and "Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled."

w.m: Matthew uses Daniel’s language, understandable to Jewish readers ("let the reader understand").
w.k: Mark also uses Daniel’s language, with the same note to the reader.
w.l: Luke explains it plainly for a Gentile audience, as the siege of Jerusalem.

groups.t: The coming of the Son of Man
groups.sh: After the distress the Son of Man will come on the clouds; learn from the fig tree.

m: Adds "the sign of the Son of Man," "all the tribes of the earth will mourn," and the trumpet call gathering the elect.
k: The most compact version.
l: Adds "distress of nations in perplexity at the roaring of the sea" and "your redemption is drawing near."

w.m: Matthew ties the coming to the nations’ mourning and the gathering of the elect.
w.k: Mark is the most compact version.
w.l: Luke focuses on hope for disciples: "lift up your heads."

groups.sh: No one knows the day or the hour; keep awake.

m: The Noah comparison and the thief at night.
k: The master leaving his house and the doorkeeper told to stay awake.
l: A warning not to be weighed down by dissipation and the cares of life.

w.m: Matthew continues with a series of parables about being ready.
w.k: Mark ends the discourse with the single word "Stay awake."
w.l: Luke ends with a call to pray for strength.

groups.sh: The chief priests and elders plan to arrest Jesus and kill him, but not during the feast.

m: Jesus first predicts that the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified at Passover.
k: A two-day countdown to Passover.
l: The leaders fear the people.
j: Told earlier, after Lazarus is raised: Caiaphas says it is better for one man to die for the people.

w.m: Matthew has Jesus announce the timeline in advance.
w.k: Mark begins his passion narrative with a two-day countdown.
w.l: Luke says they feared the people.
w.j: John turns Caiaphas’ political plan into an unwitting prophecy of Jesus’ death for the nation.

groups.sh: A woman pours expensive ointment on Jesus; some object, and Jesus defends her.

m: At the house of Simon the leper, shortly before Passover. The woman anoints his head.
k: The same setting. The woman anoints his head.
l: Much earlier, in a Pharisee’s house. A sinful woman weeps on Jesus’ feet, and the point is forgiveness, not burial. Many treat it as a different event; others see one memory told differently.
j: Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus, six days before Passover. She anoints his feet and wipes them with her hair, and Judas complains.

w.m: Matthew sets the woman’s extravagant act directly before Judas’ deal, a sharp contrast, and, like Mark, promises that her story will be told wherever the gospel is preached.
w.k: Mark places it inside the plot and betrayal, a frame of devotion between two acts of hostility.
w.l: Luke uses it to show how much forgiven sinners love.
w.j: John names Mary and Judas and links the story to Lazarus.

groups.sh: Judas goes to the chief priests and agrees to hand Jesus over.

m: Alone gives the price: thirty pieces of silver.
k: Mentions only that they promised him money.
l: "Satan entered into Judas."

w.m: Matthew’s "thirty pieces of silver" echoes Zechariah 11 and prepares for his later fulfillment quotes.
w.k: Mark states it simply.
w.l: Luke sees a cosmic struggle behind the betrayal.

groups.sh: The disciples ask where to prepare the Passover, and Jesus sends them to a certain man and a large upper room.

m: Says simply "go into the city to a certain man."
k: The sign of a man carrying a jar of water, and an upper room already furnished.
l: The same sign and room. Names Peter and John as the two sent.

w.m: Matthew shortens it.
w.k: Mark gives practical detail.
w.l: Luke names the two disciples.

groups.sh: Jesus says one of the Twelve will betray him, and each asks "Is it I?"

m: Judas asks "Is it I, Rabbi?" and Jesus replies "You have said so."
k: "One who is eating with me."
l: The announcement comes after the supper, and the disciples ask one another which of them it could be.
j: The disciple whom Jesus loved asks, and Jesus gives bread to Judas, saying "What you are going to do, do quickly."

w.m: Matthew gives a quiet exchange with Judas.
w.k: Mark has "one who is eating with me," a deeper betrayal.
w.l: Luke has the disciples ask one another which of them it could be.
w.j: John shows Jesus in control, even in the betrayal: Satan enters Judas, and "it was night."

groups.sh: Jesus takes bread and the cup, saying "This is my body" and "This is my blood of the covenant."

m: "For the forgiveness of sins." "Drink of it, all of you."
k: The shortest form: the blood "poured out for many."
l: Two cups. Adds "Do this in remembrance of me" and "the new covenant in my blood," in line with Paul (1 Corinthians 11).

w.m: Matthew spells out forgiveness as the purpose of the death.
w.k: Mark gives the shortest form, which Matthew follows closely.
w.l: Luke stresses the new covenant and remembrance for the continuing community.

groups.sh: Jesus says Peter will deny him before the rooster crows, and Peter says he never will.

m: Adds the prediction of all the disciples scattering and a promise to meet in Galilee.
k: The same, and the rooster crows "twice."
l: Jesus says "Simon, Simon, Satan demanded to sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you" and tells Peter to strengthen his brothers afterwards.
j: This happens inside the supper, after Jesus says "Where I am going you cannot come."

w.m: Matthew and Mark both quote Zechariah about striking the shepherd.
w.k: Mark has Peter’s emphatic protest.
w.l: Luke includes the prayer for Peter, which prepares for his role later.
w.j: John joins the prediction to the new commandment and the farewell discourse.

groups.sh: Jesus prays in a garden, "Not what I will, but what you will," while the disciples sleep.

m: Three prayers and three returns to the sleeping disciples.
k: Three prayers, and "Abba, Father."
l: Only one prayer. An angel strengthens him and his sweat is "like great drops of blood" (some manuscripts omit those verses). The disciples are "sleeping for sorrow."

w.m: Matthew has Jesus pray "if it be possible" and shows his humanity and obedience.
w.k: Mark has "Abba, Father," and the strongest picture of distress.
w.l: Luke shows a martyr-like prayer under strain, and makes the disciples’ failing a more sympathetic one.

groups.sh: Judas comes with a crowd and betrays Jesus with a kiss; one of the disciples strikes the high priest’s servant with a sword.

m: Adds "Put your sword back... all who take the sword will perish by the sword" and that he could call twelve legions of angels.
k: Only Mark has a young man who runs away naked.
l: Only Luke has Jesus healing the servant’s ear. "Would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?"
j: Only John names Peter as the swordsman and Malchus as the servant, and has Jesus say "I am he" so that the soldiers fall to the ground.

w.m: Matthew stresses that the Scriptures must be fulfilled and that Jesus is not a violent revolutionary.
w.k: Mark ends with a young man fleeing, a detail some think is Mark himself.
w.l: Luke has Jesus heal even the enemy, and says "this is your hour, and the power of darkness."
w.j: John shows Jesus fully in control: "Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given me?"

groups.sh: Jesus is taken to the high priest and asked whether he is the Christ.

m: A night trial before Caiaphas with false witnesses about destroying the temple. Jesus answers "You have said so," and the high priest tears his robes.
k: The same trial. Jesus answers "I am."
l: A morning meeting of the council, without false witnesses. Jesus answers "If I tell you, you will not believe."
j: Jesus is taken first to Annas, who questions him about his disciples and teaching, and sends him to Caiaphas. There is no council verdict.

w.m: Matthew says the charge is blasphemy.
w.k: Mark’s "I am" is the plainest answer.
w.l: Luke has Jesus say "from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God."
w.j: John treats the interrogation as a fair question: "If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness; but if rightly, why do you strike me?"

groups.sh: Peter denies knowing Jesus three times, and the rooster crows.

m: Peter curses and swears, then weeps bitterly.
k: Peter curses and swears.
l: Only Luke says "the Lord turned and looked at Peter."
j: Peter is at the fire with "another disciple" known to the high priest. The third challenger is a relative of the man whose ear Peter cut off.

w.m: Matthew sets the denial against Jesus’ earlier warning about denying him before others (10:33); Peter “wept bitterly.”
w.k: Tradition links Mark’s Gospel to Peter’s own preaching, and some find his memory behind this honest account.
w.l: Luke focuses on the look that breaks Peter.
w.j: John ties it to the arrest scene, and will balance it with Peter’s restoration at the lake (21:15–19).

groups.sh: Pilate asks "Are you the King of the Jews?" and Jesus says "You have said so."

m: Brief. Judas’ death and the field of blood come between the council and Pilate.
k: Only the essentials. Jesus’ silence amazes Pilate.
l: Names the charges (misleading the nation, opposing taxes, claiming to be Christ a king) and adds the trip to Herod.
j: A long dialogue about kingship ("My kingdom is not of this world"; "What is truth?"). The Jewish leaders do not enter the Gentile’s headquarters, to avoid defilement before Passover.

w.m: Matthew adds Judas’ suicide and the field of blood.
w.k: Mark gives only the essentials; Jesus’ silence amazes Pilate.
w.l: Luke has Pilate declare "I find no guilt in this man."
w.j: John makes the trial a debate about truth and kingship.

groups.sh: Pilate offers to release Barabbas or Jesus, and the crowd chooses Barabbas.

m: Alone has Pilate’s wife’s dream, Pilate washing his hands, and the crowd’s "His blood be on us and on our children."
k: Pilate wants to satisfy the crowd.
l: Pilate declares Jesus innocent three times.
j: Pilate has Jesus flogged, presents him ("Behold the man!"), and the leaders say "We have no king but Caesar."

w.m: Matthew shows Pilate as reluctant, and places responsibility on the people.
w.k: Mark has Pilate wanting to satisfy the crowd.
w.l: Luke stresses Jesus’ innocence, as he does in the rest of the passion.
w.j: John uses it as a drama about who is truly king.

groups.sh: Soldiers put a purple robe and crown of thorns on Jesus and mock him as king.

m: Adds a reed in his right hand, and the soldiers strike his head with it. A scarlet robe.
k: The whole battalion is called. A purple robe.
j: The flogging and mocking come before Pilate’s final verdict. Luke has no scene of Roman soldiers mocking here; Herod’s soldiers mock him earlier (23:11).

w.m: Matthew has a scarlet robe and the reed, a mock scepter.
w.k: Mark says the whole battalion was called.
w.j: John makes the mockery a throne scene: "Hail, King of the Jews."

groups.sh: Jesus is led out and crucified at Golgotha; Simon of Cyrene carries the cross.

m: Wine mixed with gall is offered.
k: Names Simon’s sons, Alexander and Rufus.
l: Adds the women of Jerusalem weeping and Jesus’ words "weep for yourselves and for your children."
j: Jesus carries his own cross; Simon is not mentioned.

w.m: Matthew mentions wine mixed with gall, echoing Psalm 69.
w.k: Mark names Simon’s sons, perhaps because they were known to Mark’s readers.
w.l: Luke adds the mourning women and a warning about Jerusalem.
w.j: John has Jesus carrying the cross himself, a sign of his control.

groups.sh: Jesus is crucified between two others, with a sign above him, and soldiers divide his clothes.

m: Both thieves mock him. The sign: "This is Jesus, the King of the Jews."
k: Both thieves mock him. The sign: "The King of the Jews." Gives the third hour.
l: Alone has "Father, forgive them" and the repentant thief ("Today you will be with me in paradise"). The sign: "This is the King of the Jews."
j: Alone has Jesus giving his mother to the beloved disciple and the soldiers casting lots for the seamless tunic. The sign, "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews," is in three languages.

w.m: Matthew shows the full mockery of leaders and passers-by.
w.k: Mark times the crucifixion at the third hour.
w.l: Luke makes the cross a place of forgiveness and promise.
w.j: John shows Jesus caring for his mother.

groups.sh: Darkness covers the land, Jesus dies, the temple curtain is torn, and the centurion responds.

m: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" Only Matthew has the earthquake, opened tombs and raised saints. The centurion: "Truly this was the Son of God."
k: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" The centurion: "Truly this man was the Son of God."
l: "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit." The centurion: "Certainly this man was innocent."
j: "I thirst" and "It is finished," and the piercing of his side with blood and water.

w.m: Matthew stresses cosmic signs that mark the end of the old age.
w.k: Mark has the loud cry and the centurion’s confession as the answer to the question of the whole Gospel.
w.l: Luke shows a peaceful trust and a repentant crowd.
w.j: John shows Jesus completing his work ("It is finished") and fulfilling Scripture.

groups.sh: Joseph of Arimathea asks Pilate for the body and lays it in a new tomb.

m: Joseph is rich and a disciple, and the tomb is his own.
k: Alone says Pilate wondered whether Jesus was already dead.
l: Joseph is a good and righteous man who had not consented to the council’s decision.
j: Nicodemus brings about seventy-five pounds of spices, and they wrap the body in linen with the spices.

w.m: Matthew sets up the guard at the tomb (27:62–66).
w.k: Mark mentions the centurion confirming the death.
w.l: Luke says Joseph was a good and righteous man who had not consented to the council’s decision.
w.j: John makes the burial a royal one, with Nicodemus.

groups.sh: On the first day of the week women go to the tomb and find the stone rolled away; Jesus is risen.

m: One angel. The women meet Jesus on the way and hold his feet.
k: One young man. The earliest manuscripts end at 16:8 with the women afraid.
l: Two men in dazzling clothes.
j: Mary Magdalene goes alone and tells Peter and the other disciple, who run to the tomb. She sees two angels, then meets Jesus, who says "Do not cling to me."

w.m: Matthew adds an earthquake and the guard, and a command to go to Galilee.
w.k: Mark ends with surprising silence, leaving the reader to respond.
w.l: Luke has the women remember Jesus’ own words and the apostles doubt.
w.j: John shows a personal encounter: Jesus calls Mary by name.

groups.sh: Jesus appears to two disciples walking to a village.

k: A two-verse summary in the longer ending. The others did not believe them.
l: Tells the whole story, including the disciples’ recognition at the breaking of the bread.

w.k: Mark’s later ending summarizes appearances in a few lines.
w.l: Luke shows Jesus teaching the Scriptures and recognized in the meal, as a pattern for the church.

groups.sh: On the evening of Easter Jesus appears to the disciples; "Peace be with you."

k: Mentions only that he rebuked their unbelief.
l: Jesus shows his hands and feet and eats broiled fish.
j: Jesus shows his hands and side, breathes on them, and gives the Holy Spirit and authority to forgive.

w.k: Mark’s later ending points to unbelief.
w.l: Luke stresses a physical body and the fulfillment of Scripture.
w.j: John makes the scene a commissioning in the Spirit.

groups.sh: Jesus sends his followers out with his authority.

m: The Great Commission on a mountain in Galilee: "Go and make disciples of all nations... I am with you always."
k: The longer ending: "Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel," with signs that follow believers.
l: Repentance and forgiveness will be proclaimed to all nations beginning in Jerusalem. Ends with the ascension at Bethany.

w.m: Matthew ends on a mountain, with a promise of presence.
w.k: Mark’s longer ending, which many scholars think was added later, shows the Lord working with them.
w.l: Luke ends with joy in the temple and leads into Acts.
